# Full content

What follows is the complete text of the site's buying guides, plus the current inventory as of this build.


## What does “scratch-and-dent” actually mean?

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/scratch-and-dent/

A scratch-and-dent appliance is a brand-new unit with cosmetic damage — a dented side panel, a scratched door, a scuff from a forklift. It was never used. It works exactly like the pristine one on the showroom floor. It just can't be sold at full price anymore, so it sells for hundreds less.
That's the entire business model behind Cade's Liquidation: buy these units by the truckload, test every one, and sell them for a fraction of retail.


### Why is it so much cheaper?

When a $1,500 refrigerator gets a dent in the side during shipping, the big-box store can't put it back on the floor at full price. It goes to a liquidation sale, where buyers bid on entire truckloads. The per-unit cost ends up far below wholesale — and that discount gets passed on to you. It's common to save 30% or more off retail, sometimes over half.


### What does the damage actually look like?

Almost always, it's on the sides or back — the parts you never see once the appliance is installed. A refrigerator slides between cabinets. A washer sits in a laundry room. A range backs up to a wall. The front — the part you actually look at every day — is usually flawless.
Every listing on this site has real photos of the actual unit, so you can see exactly what you're getting before you ever come look at it.
And here's the oldest trick in the book: got a small dent somewhere visible? Stick a magnet over it. A photo, a kid's drawing, a pizza coupon — done. Most of our customers do exactly that on day one and never think about the dent again.


### Buy the nicer appliance for the same money

Here's the move most of our customers figure out fast: a scratch-and-dent $1,400 French-door refrigerator for $700 beats a brand-new $700 top-freezer every single time. Same money out of your pocket — twice the appliance. The dent lives on the side you'll never see; the ice maker, the water dispenser, and the extra space are what you live with every day.
Scratch-and-dent flips the normal math. Instead of asking “what can I afford?”, ask “what's the nicest unit I can get for my budget?” You'll almost always land one or two tiers higher than buying new — and nobody has ever come back wishing they'd bought the cheaper one.


### What's not wrong with them

Scratch-and-dent does not mean used, refurbished, or repaired. These units were never owned by anyone. Nothing was broken and fixed. The compressor, the motor, the heating element — all factory-new, all covered by the same 14-day money-back guarantee as everything else here.


### How every unit gets checked

Before anything gets listed, it's unboxed, plugged in, and run through its paces — washers run a cycle, dryers heat up, refrigerators get cold, ovens hit temperature. If a unit doesn't work like new, it doesn't get listed. Cosmetic damage is the deal; mechanical problems are a deal-breaker.


## Washer buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/washers/

A washing machine is one of those purchases you live with for a decade, so it's worth spending ten minutes learning what matters. The good news: washers are simple machines, and there are only a few decisions that actually count.


### Top-load vs. front-load

Top-load with agitator — the classic. Fast cycles, simple to use, and you can toss in a forgotten sock mid-cycle. Harder on clothes and uses more water.
Top-load with impeller (no agitator) — gentler and roomier than agitator models, but longer cycles.
Front-load — the most efficient and gentlest on clothes, with the biggest capacities. The trade-off: you should leave the door cracked between loads so the gasket dries out.


### What to check before you buy

Run a quick cycle — it should fill, agitate or tumble, drain, and spin without banging around.
On front-loaders, check the door gasket for tears or mold.
Make sure the hoses (or hookups) are included or plan to buy new ones — they're cheap insurance.
Excessive shaking during spin usually means an unbalanced load, not a bad machine — but it shouldn't walk across the floor.


### Measuring your space

Standard washers are about 27 inches wide. Measure your laundry nook's width, then measure the doorways and hallways the machine has to travel through — that's the measurement people forget. For top-loaders, check there's clearance above to open the lid; for front-loaders, make sure the door can swing open fully.


### Spend a little more, get a lot more

If a front-loader is only slightly more than the top-load you're eyeing, take the front-loader — gentler on clothes, bigger loads, lower water bills, and you'll use it for the next decade. And if you're buying a dryer too, grab them as a pair: bundling knocks up to 15% off, which usually covers the step up to the nicer model by itself.


### Capacity

Measured in cubic feet. Around 4.5 cu. ft. and up handles a family comfortably, including bulky items like comforters. Smaller households can get by with less, but bigger tubs are more forgiving — overstuffing is what wears machines out.


## Dryer buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/dryers/

Dryers are even simpler than washers — but there's one decision that matters more than everything else combined: gas or electric. Get that right and the rest is easy.


### Gas vs. electric — the big decision

Gas dryers cost more up front but are cheaper to run, and they heat up faster. They need a gas line in the laundry room.
Electric dryers cost less to buy but need a 240-volt outlet — not a regular wall plug.
The practical rule: buy whatever your laundry room already has. Running a new gas line or wiring a 240V circuit costs far more than any savings from switching fuel types. If you're not sure what you have, text a photo of the hookups and we'll help you figure it out.


### What to check before you buy

It should produce real heat on every heat setting — no heat usually means a dead heating element or igniter.
The drum should turn smoothly without grinding or squealing.
Check the lint trap slides in and out and isn't cracked.
Make sure the timer or electronic controls advance through a cycle.


### Measuring your space

Like washers, standard dryers are about 27 inches wide. Allow a few extra inches of depth for the vent hose behind the machine, and check the door swing. If you're buying a washer and dryer together, matching widths look right and fit the space evenly.


### Buy the pair, save on both

Here's the thing about dryers: the smartest money isn't in the dryer, it's in the pair. A matching washer and dryer bought together with the bundle discount (up to 15% off) often costs less than buying them one at a time — which means the nicer dryer you were debating basically pays for itself. Match your washer's width, pick your fuel type, and bundle them.


### Venting

Almost every home dryer in the US is vented — it needs a duct to the outside. Keep that duct short and clean; a clogged vent is the #1 reason dryers underperform and the #1 laundry-room fire hazard.


## Refrigerator buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/refrigerators/

The refrigerator is the hardest-working appliance in your home — it runs 24/7 for a decade or more. Here's how to pick the right type, check that it works, and make sure it actually fits through your front door.


### The four types

French door — double doors up top, freezer drawer below. The most popular style: wide shelves fit platters and pizza boxes, and you only open half the fridge at a time.
Side-by-side — fridge on one side, freezer on the other. Narrow doors are great for tight kitchens, but wide items don't fit.
Top-freezer — the classic. The most refrigerator for the money and the most reliable layout ever made.
Bottom-freezer — fresh food at eye level, freezer in a pull-out drawer below. A nice middle ground.


### What to check before you buy

It should be genuinely cold — fridge around 37°F, freezer at 0°F. Every unit here is plugged in and tested before listing.
If it has an ice maker or water dispenser, run both.
Check the door seals: close the door on a dollar bill — if it slides out easily, the seal is weak.
Look for excessive frost in the freezer, which can signal a seal or defrost issue.


### Measuring your space

This is where most refrigerator purchases go wrong. Measure width, height (including the hinge!), and depth of the opening. Then measure your doorways and hallways — a 36-inch-wide fridge does not fit through a 32-inch door, and the doors usually come off to buy you a couple of inches. Decide between counter-depth (flush with cabinets, less capacity) and standard depth (sticks out a few inches, holds more).


### This is where scratch-and-dent wins biggest

Refrigerators are the category where the scratch-and-dent math is most dramatic. The jump from a basic top-freezer to a French door changes your daily life — wide shelves, ice and water in the door, a freezer drawer that actually organizes. And a dented French door routinely costs the same as a pristine basic model. Buy the nicer fridge. The dent lives on the side; the convenience lives in your kitchen.


### Features: worth it or not?

Ice and water in the door are genuinely convenient — and the most common thing to need a repair down the road. Door-in-door and smart screens are nice but add cost and complexity. For pure reliability-per-dollar, a basic top-freezer is almost impossible to beat.


## Range buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/ranges/

The range is the centerpiece of the kitchen — and the appliance where the fuel question matters most, because cooks have strong opinions about it. Here's the practical version.


### Gas vs. electric

Gas — instant heat, instant off, visible flame. Preferred by most serious cooks. Needs a gas line behind the stove.
Electric smooth-top — sleek, easy to wipe clean, very even oven heat. Needs a 240-volt outlet.
Electric coil — the budget workhorse. Cheap, repairable, and nearly indestructible.
Same rule as dryers: match what's already in your kitchen. Running a gas line or a 240V circuit just to switch fuels rarely pays off.


### What to check before you buy

Every burner or element should heat — test all of them, not just one.
The oven should reach temperature (every oven here is tested before listing).
On gas ranges, the igniter should click and light promptly on every burner.
Check the oven door seal and that storage drawers slide freely.


### Measuring your space

The standard range is 30 inches wide. Measure your opening, and check the depth including the handle — that's the part that sticks out into the walkway. Confirm whether you have a gas hookup or a 240V outlet before you fall in love with a unit.


### The upgrade worth paying for

If there's one step-up worth the money on a range, it's convection — faster, more even cooking you'll notice every single week. Thanks to scratch-and-dent pricing, a convection range with a scuffed side panel typically costs about what a basic coil-top model does new. Same budget, much better cooking.


### Nice-to-have features

Convection fans cook faster and more evenly — genuinely useful. Air-fry modes are a fun bonus on newer models. Self-cleaning is convenient but hard on the oven's electronics over time; many techs quietly recommend against using it often.


## Freezer buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/freezers/

A second freezer is one of the best money-saving appliances there is — buy in bulk, freeze garden produce, and stop throwing food away. Here's how to pick the right one.


### Chest vs. upright

Chest freezers give you the most space per dollar, hold their cold better during power outages (cold air sinks and stays put when you open the lid), and are dead simple mechanically. The downside: things get buried — use bins to stay organized.
Upright freezers work like a refrigerator: shelves, easy to see everything, no digging. They cost more per cubic foot and lose more cold air when opened, but most people find them far easier to live with.


### Garage-ready matters

Not every freezer is designed to run in an unheated garage. Standard models can struggle or shut down when ambient temperatures drop near freezing. If yours is going in the garage, look for one rated “garage ready” — it's built to handle Illinois winters.


### What to check before you buy

It should reach 0°F and hold it. Every freezer here is plugged in and tested before listing.
Check the lid or door seal all the way around — a weak seal is the main cause of frost buildup.
Look inside for rust or heavy staining, which can signal a hard previous life.


### Chest or upright? Be honest with yourself

Chest freezers win on price per cubic foot — but here's the honest truth: food you can't see is food you'll forget, and forgotten food is money in the trash. If the budget stretches, the upright is the freezer you'll actually enjoy owning. An organized upright wastes less food, which quietly pays you back all year.


### Where to put it

Freezers need a few inches of airflow around them and a level spot. Measure the space and the path getting it there — chest freezers are bulky and awkward to move. If you need it delivered, that's what we're here for.


## Dishwasher buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/dishwashers/

Dishwashers all look the same from the outside, which is why most people buy blind and hope. Don't — there are really only three things that separate a great dishwasher from a loud, damp disappointment.


### The three things that matter

1. Noise (dBA). This is the spec that affects your daily life most. Under 45 dBA is whisper-quiet; around 50 is normal conversation level and fine for most homes; above 55 you'll hear it from the next room.
2. Tub material. Stainless steel tubs handle higher heat, which means better drying and less odor over time. Plastic tubs cost less but leave dishes damper.
3. The third rack. That skinny top rack for utensils and lids frees up a surprising amount of room below. Once you've had one, you won't go back.


### What to check before you buy

Run a full cycle and check for leaks underneath — this is the big one.
Racks should slide smoothly and spray arms should spin freely.
The door should latch firmly and the gasket should be intact all the way around.


### Measuring your space

Standard dishwashers are 24 inches wide and slide into a cabinet opening — measure the opening, not the old dishwasher. Check that you have the water line, drain hookup, and power already in place; they're usually there if a dishwasher was installed before.


### The upgrade customers are happiest they made

Ask anyone who owns one: the two things worth paying extra for in a dishwasher are quietness (under 50 dBA) and a stainless tub. You'll run this machine nearly every day for a decade — the difference between hearing it from the couch and forgetting it's on is worth every penny. This is the single most no-regrets upgrade in the appliance world.


### A note on installation

Swapping a dishwasher involves water, drain, and electrical connections under your sink. If that doesn't sound like your idea of a Saturday, installation services are available — just ask for a quote.


## Wall oven buying guide

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/ovens/

Wall ovens are the most measurement-sensitive appliance you can buy — they have to fit a precise cabinet cutout. Get the measuring right and everything else is straightforward.


### Single vs. double

Single ovens fit standard cutouts and handle nearly everything a home cook needs. Double ovens are a dream for holidays and big families — two temperatures at once — but they need a taller cutout and cost significantly more. Combination microwave/oven units pack both into one cutout and are worth a look during a kitchen remodel.


### Gas vs. electric

The vast majority of wall ovens are electric, and electricity is arguably better for baking anyway — drier, more even heat. Gas wall ovens exist but are uncommon; check your hookup before assuming.


### Measure twice, buy once

This is the whole game with wall ovens. Measure the cabinet cutout's width, height, and depth — not the old oven, the hole it sits in. Manufacturers publish exact cutout specs, and there's very little forgiveness. When in doubt, text us the measurements and we'll confirm fit before you buy.


### Worth the step up

If you're choosing between a basic single oven and a convection or double oven for similar money, take the nicer one — you'll cook on it for 15 years. Holiday cooking with two temperatures at once is one of those things you don't know you needed until you've had it.


### What to check before you buy

The oven should reach and hold temperature — every oven here is tested before listing.
Check the door seal and that the door closes flush.
Test all controls and any convection fan.


## Delivery & service area

URL: https://cadesliquidation.com/guides/delivery/

You found the appliance. Now let's get it to your house. Delivery is simple: $50 flat, delivered to your door anywhere in Bloomington-Normal, IL.


### How delivery works

Pick your appliance — browse the catalog and text or call to claim it.
Schedule a time — we'll find a delivery window that works for you.
We bring it to your door — $50 flat within Bloomington-Normal, IL.


### Outside Bloomington-Normal?

No problem — we deliver to surrounding communities all the time. Text or call for a quote; the price depends on distance. (Delivery costs move with fuel prices, so we quote each trip individually rather than posting a rate that goes stale.)


### Installation services

Need it hooked up, not just dropped off? Installation services are available for an additional charge — dishwashers, ranges, over-the-range microwaves, and more. Text for pricing; we'll tell you straight whether your setup is simple or complicated before you commit to anything.


### Prefer to pick up?

You're welcome to come see everything in person first — the warehouse is open by appointment. Call or text to schedule a time, and we'll have the unit pulled out and ready when you arrive.
